title.en: Voxel grid with explicit index-to-world ownership

summary: Treat a voxel grid as integer indices plus a declared transform, and keep occupancy, sampled values and their sampling positions distinct.
objective: A named cell resolves to one world position under the declared transform, and moving the grid moves the data with it without changing any stored value.
intent_signals: my heat values are offset by half a cell
how big is one voxel in metres
store a field on a grid
the volume shifts when I move the object
example_prompts: Build a voxel packing tray where each cell has a definite size.
Store a temperature field on a grid and let me probe a cell.
Show which cells are occupied and which are merely defined.
negative_signals: unstructured triangle mesh from a scanner
continuous analytic surface with no sampling
not_for: Surface-only assets, where a mesh carries the shape directly.
Solver results that must remain on their original unstructured or adaptive mesh.

principles: A voxel grid is two separate things: integer indices that address storage, and a transform that says where those indices sit in the world. Confusing them makes every later measurement ambiguous.
Occupancy and value are different questions. A cell can be defined and empty, defined and zero, or outside the stored region entirely, and the presentation must be able to tell them apart.
Say whether a stored number describes the cell as a whole or the lattice point at its corner. A half-cell offset between the two conventions is the most common silent error in voxel visualisation.
Voxel size is a modelling decision with visible consequences: it sets the smallest feature that can exist, the staircase amplitude on any diagonal surface and the memory cost of the field.

Most interesting volumes are mostly empty. Storing a default background value and only the deviations from it is a representation choice that should be stated, because it changes what iteration over the grid means.
implementation: Record the grid origin, the voxel spacing and the axis order once, and derive every world position from that record instead of hard-coding offsets at each use site.
Provide both directions of the mapping: index to world for placing geometry and labels, and world to index for probing, picking and brush-style editing.
For interpolated lookups, convert the world position into continuous index coordinates first and interpolate there, so a fractional index has a defined meaning between neighbouring samples.
Keep an explicit active or occupied marker separate from the stored value, and make the legend distinguish empty, zero and undefined.
Render solid voxels as merged surfaces where the object reads better as a shape, and as individual cells where the discreteness is the point; state which reading the scene is using.
When the grid represents measured or computed data, keep the units and the value range with the grid, and do not rescale values silently to fit a colour ramp.
observable_checks: Probing a named cell reports the same world position that the rendered cell occupies, and the reported index round-trips back to the same cell.
Translating or rotating the grid moves the rendered volume without changing any reported stored value.
Halving the voxel size doubles the resolution of the visible staircase on a diagonal boundary and does not shift the surface by half a cell.
Empty, zero and undefined cells are visually distinguishable, and the legend names all three.

A value probed at a stored sample location, meaning the cell centre or the lattice node according to the convention the record declares, matches the stored value exactly; probes between sample locations follow the declared interpolation rule rather than returning a stored value.

creative_affordances: The cell grid can be celebrated rather than hidden: chamfered cells, gapped lattices and coloured strata are all legitimate voxel looks.
A coarse grid chosen for readability is a valid design decision when the record says the resolution is expressive rather than measured.
known_limits: This profile governs the grid and its addressing. It does not make any stored field physically meaningful and does not perform any simulation.
The index-and-transform model cited here comes from one sparse-volume library's documentation; other toolkits use different conventions for where a sample sits inside a cell.
Authored reusable guidance; no runtime artifact or rendered result has been observed for this record.

claims.statement: A sparse volume library addresses its samples with unit-less signed integer index coordinates and relies on a separate transform to place them in world space, generalising the lattice to a continuous index space so that fractional index coordinates carry meaning for interpolation, and providing explicit index-to-world and world-to-index conversions including a cell-centred variant.
claims.scope: Documented data model of the OpenVDB library as of the access date. It establishes that index addressing and physical placement are separate concerns; it does not standardise voxel conventions across other toolkits.
